title: Bellarmine: adversaries confuse faith-certainty with trust-certainty
source_text: XII. Ita philosophatur hac de re Bellarminus, lib. 3. de Justif. cap. 2. sub finem, Deinde. Adversarii, inquit, ut fidem cum fiducia, ita certitudinem fidei cum certitudine fiduciae confundunt. Multum autem interest inter utramque certitudinem. Nam certitudo fidei, quae nititur sola Dei authoritate, omni ex parte dubitationem excludit. Certitudo fiduciae partim nititur divina promissione, partim propria dispositione: & quod attinet ad divinam promissionem, omnem similiter formidinem excludit, & est absolute, & simpliciter certitudo; quod attinet ad propriam dispositionem, non excludit quidem penitus formidinem, neque est certitudo simpliciter, sed secundum quid, & conjecturalis; tamen tanta est, ut satis esse possit ad securitatem gignendam. Quae eadem fusius persequitur atque amplificat ejusdem libri cap. 11. Quod autem. Ubi praeterea observat duplicem in spe certitudinem considerari posse: unam ex parte intellectus, quam modo verbis illius descripsimus; alteram ex parte voluntatis, quae est firma adhaesio voluntatis ad rem speratam: quae maxima esse potest, etiamsi ex parte intellectus non sit homo certus se rem illam consecuturum. Certitudo vero illa quae in fide est, solum intellectum afficit.
pass_a_gloss: So Bellarmine philosophizes on this matter in On Justification, book 3, chapter 2, toward the end, at ‘Then.’ The adversaries, he says, as they confuse faith with trust, so confuse the certainty of faith with the certainty of trust. But there is a great difference between the two certainties. For the certainty of faith, which rests on God’s authority alone, excludes doubt on every side. The certainty of trust rests partly on the divine promise, partly on one’s own disposition: and as regards the divine promise, it likewise excludes every fear and is absolutely and simply certainty; as regards one’s own disposition, it does not indeed exclude fear altogether, nor is it certainty simply, but in a qualified sense and conjectural; yet it is so great that it can suffice to beget security. Which same points he pursues more fully and amplifies in chapter 11 of the same book, at ‘But what.’ Where moreover he observes that a double certainty can be considered in hope: one on the side of the intellect, which we have just described in his words; the other on the side of the will, which is a firm adhesion of the will to the thing hoped for—which can be very great even if on the side of the intellect a person is not certain he will obtain that thing. But that certainty which is in faith affects the intellect alone.
pass_b_english: Bellarmine charges Protestants with confusing faith-certainty and trust-certainty.
Trust is absolute on the promise side but only conjectural about one’s disposition, yet still enough for security; faith’s certainty touches intellect alone.
